pos: n. (eldest son of Levi, and the Levitical family charged with the curtains and coverings of the tabernacle — the carriers of the fabric of the house of God)
etymology: From Hebrew Gershon or Gershom, probably from garash, to drive out or expel — the same root behind the name Moses gave his own son, “a stranger in a strange land”. The gentilic is Gershonite.
biblical_def: Gershon was the firstborn of Levi — “and the sons of Levi; Gershon, Kohath, and Merari” (Gen 46:11) — and gave his name to one of the three Levitical divisions that carried the tabernacle through the wilderness. The division of labour is exact and it is worth attending to. Kohath, the second son, carried the holy things: the ark, the table, the candlestick, the altars, borne on the shoulder and never touched. Merari carried the frame: boards, bars, pillars, sockets, and the wagons for them. And “the charge of the sons of Gershon in the tabernacle of the congregation shall be the tabernacle, and the tent, the covering thereof, and the hanging for the door” (Num 3:25) — the curtains, the coverings of rams' skins and badgers' skins, the hangings of the court, the cords. Their commission is summarised in six words: “This is the service of the families of the Gershonites, to serve, and for burdens” (Num 4:24). They were the oldest branch and they were given the cloth, not the gold; two covered wagons and four oxen; and they pitched behind the tabernacle westward. Under David the Gershonites appear among the singers and over the treasures of the house of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Gershon; in sacred history he is the eldest son of Levi, from whom the Gershonites, one of the three great Levitical families, are named.
webster_full: GERSHON, n. The eldest son of Levi, also written Gershom; the name is thought to signify expulsion or a stranger.
From him descended the Gershonites, one of the three families of the tribe of Levi.
Their charge in the wilderness was the tabernacle and the tent, the coverings, hangings and cords.
They were given two wagons and four oxen for the carriage of their burden, and pitched westward behind the tabernacle.
In the days of David certain of the Gershonites were set over the treasures of the house of the Lord.
scriptures: And the sons of Levi; Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Exo 6:16
And these are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations; Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari: and the years of the life of Levi were an hundred thirty and seven years.
Num 3:25

And the charge of the sons of Gershon in the tabernacle of the congregation shall be the tabernacle, and the tent, the covering thereof, and the hanging for the door of the tabernacle of the congregation,
Num 4:24
This is the service of the families of the Gershonites, to serve, and for burdens:
corruption_summary: Assigned, unglamorous service is treated as a lesser calling; the eldest son of Levi was given the curtains, and Scripture records his charge in the same breath and the same detail as the ark.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of appointed service. Gershon was Levi's firstborn and did not get the ark; a younger brother's house carried the holy things on their shoulders while Gershon's house folded curtains onto wagons. Nothing in the text treats this as a demotion. The Holy Ghost specifies the badgers' skins and the cords with the same seriousness as the mercy seat, because in the worship of God the question is never how visible the office is but whether the man is doing the thing appointed to him. Paul argues it at length in 1Co 12, and gives the conclusion: “God hath set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him” (1Co 12:18).

The second lesson is in the phrase “to serve, and for burdens.” Levitical work was heavy, unromantic, physical labour: hauling wet skins, coiling cords, loading oxen, and doing it again at the next encampment. The New Testament keeps the register — deacons, helps, governments, bearing one another's burdens. A congregation that can only recruit for the visible ministries and cannot find men to carry the coverings has misunderstood what the house of God has always required.
roots_summary: Hebrew Gershon / Gershom (H1648, H1647), from garash (H1644), to drive out; mishkan (H4908), tabernacle; massa' (H4853), a burden.
roots_lines: Hebrew Gershon (H1648) — Gershon; the firstborn of Levi, ancestor of the Gershonites.
Hebrew garash (H1644) — to drive out, expel; the likely root, sounding the theme of sojourn.
Hebrew mishkan (H4908) — the tabernacle, a dwelling place; the fabric structure in Gershon's charge.
Hebrew 'ohel (H168) — the tent; the goats' hair covering spread over the tabernacle.
Hebrew massa' (H4853) — a burden, that which is lifted; the word of Num 4:24, service defined as load-bearing.
usage: “The sons of Levi; Gershon, Kohath, and Merari” — the three divisions of the sanctuary's service.
“The tabernacle, and the tent, the covering thereof” — a charge itemised by God.
“To serve, and for burdens” — the whole commission in six words.

pos: n. (youngest son of Kohath and uncle of Aaron — whose sons carried their cousins' bodies out of the camp after the strange fire)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Uzzi'el, “God is my strength”, from 'oz, strength, and 'El, God. The gentilic is Uzzielite. Several later Levites and one goldsmith of Nehemiah's wall bear the name.
biblical_def: Uzziel was the fourth and youngest son of Kohath — “and the sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel” (Exo 6:18) — and so the uncle of Aaron and Moses. His own sons were “Mishael, and Elzaphan, and Zithri” (Exo 6:22), and two of them are called on at the most dreadful moment in the history of the priesthood. Nadab and Abihu had offered strange fire before the LORD and fire had gone out and devoured them; Aaron and his surviving sons were forbidden to mourn or to leave the sanctuary. So Moses sent for the cousins: “Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said unto them, Come near, carry your brethren from before the sanctuary out of the camp” (Lev 10:4). They carried the bodies out in their coats. Elzaphan afterwards became chief of the whole Kohathite house (Num 3:30), set over the ark and the holy furniture. The Uzzielites number three hundred and twelve men in the wilderness census and appear again under David among the Levites David gathered to bring the ark up to Jerusalem the second and lawful time.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Uzziel; in sacred history he is the youngest son of Kohath and uncle of Aaron, father of the Uzzielite family of Levites.
webster_full: UZZIEL, n. The son of Kohath and brother of Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron; the name signifies God is my strength.
His sons were Mishael, Elzaphan and Zithri.
Mishael and Elzaphan carried the bodies of Nadab and Abihu out of the camp at the command of Moses.
Elzaphan was made chief of the families of the Kohathites.
The Uzzielites were numbered in the wilderness, and served in the house of the Lord in the days of David and Hezekiah.
scriptures: Exo 6:18
And the sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel: and the years of the life of Kohath were an hundred thirty and three years.
Exo 6:22
And the sons of Uzziel; Mishael, and Elzaphan, and Zithri.
Lev 10:4
And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said unto them, Come near, carry your brethren from before the sanctuary out of the camp.
Num 3:30
And the chief of the house of the father of the families of the Kohathites shall be Elizaphan the son of Uzziel.
corruption_summary: The death of Nadab and Abihu is read as divine overreaction; Scripture presents it as the founding case for the regulative principle — worship God has not commanded is forbidden, however sincere.
corruption_paragraphs: Uzziel's sons carried out the bodies, so his family is bound to Leviticus 10, and that chapter is the hardest one in the Bible on the subject of worship. Nadab and Abihu offered incense with fire the LORD “commanded them not” (Lev 10:1). They were priests; the incense was real incense; the altar was the right altar; the God was the true God. The one defect was that this particular act had not been commanded. The modern objection — that God is unreasonably severe about a technicality — assumes worship is an offering of our sincerity, so that the form is incidental. Scripture assumes the opposite: worship is an approach to a holy God on terms He sets, and the terms are the mercy. This is the regulative principle the Reformed churches confess: what Scripture commands in worship is required, and what it has not commanded is not permitted.

The second thing in Lev 10 is the vocation given to Uzziel's sons, and it is a sober one. Somebody has to carry the bodies out. Aaron and his remaining sons could not; they were under oil and could not leave the door. So the cousins came near, took hold of coats, and did the worst job in Israel that day without a word recorded. There is a ministry of removing the wreckage after a judgment falls in a congregation — a discipline case, a fallen pastor, a scandal — and it is done by men who did not cause it and will get no credit for it. God names them.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Uzzi'el (H5816), from 'oz (H5797), strength, and 'El (H410), God; 'esh zarah (H784 + H2114), strange fire.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Uzzi'el (H5816) — Uzziel, “God is my strength”; youngest son of Kohath.
Hebrew 'oz (H5797) — strength, might, boldness; the first element of the name.
Hebrew 'Eltsaphan (H469) — Elzaphan or Elizaphan, “God has hidden”; his son, made chief of the Kohathites.
Hebrew 'esh zarah — strange fire; fire the LORD “commanded them not” (Lev 10:1).
Hebrew tsawah (H6680) — to command, charge; the verb whose absence condemned Nadab and Abihu.
usage: “The sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel” — the four branches of the holiest house.
“The sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron” — kinsmen called to a terrible errand.
“Carry your brethren from before the sanctuary” — the office of clearing away a judgment.

pos: n. (son of Kohath, husband of Jochebed, and father of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam — the man whose household produced Israel's prophet, priest, and prophetess)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Amram, probably “exalted people” or “the kinsman is exalted”, from 'am, people or kinsman, and rum, to be high. The gentilic is Amramite.
biblical_def: Amram is the father of the three people through whom the exodus came. “And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years” (Exo 6:20); Numbers adds the daughter: “she bare unto Amram Aaron and Moses, and Miriam their sister” (Num 26:59). From one Levite household came the high priest, the lawgiver, and the prophetess who led the women at the Red Sea. Of Amram himself Scripture records no speech and no act — except one, and Hebrews supplies it: “By faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king's commandment” (Heb 11:23). Amram and Jochebed defied a royal infanticide order and hid a baby, and the New Testament calls that faith and puts them in the roll of the believing. The one thing the Bible tells us Amram did with his life was to refuse to hand over his son to be killed. His line ran on: “the children of Amram; Aaron, and Moses, and Miriam” (1Ch 6:3), and after them Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, and the whole Aaronic priesthood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Amram; in sacred history he is the son of Kohath and father of Aaron, Moses and Miriam by Jochebed his father's sister.
webster_full: AMRAM, n. The son of Kohath, the son of Levi, and the father of Aaron, Moses and Miriam.
He married Jochebed his father's sister, before the law forbidding such marriage was given.
He lived a hundred and thirty and seven years.
His family, the Amramites, was one of the four houses of the Kohathites.
By faith he and his wife hid their child three months, not fearing the commandment of the king.
scriptures: Exo 6:20
And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years.
And the name of Amram's wife was Jochebed, the daughter of Levi, whom her mother bare to Levi in Egypt: and she bare unto Amram Aaron and Moses, and Miriam their sister.
And the children of Amram; Aaron, and Moses, and Miriam. The sons also of Aaron; Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
Exo 6:18
And the sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel: and the years of the life of Kohath were an hundred thirty and three years.
corruption_summary: Amram's marriage to his aunt is cited as proof that biblical morality shifts with convenience; the law forbidding it had not yet been given, and Scripture is transparent about the sequence rather than hiding it.
corruption_paragraphs: Amram married his father's sister, and Lev 18:12 later forbids exactly that: “Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's sister.” The point is regularly offered as a contradiction, or as evidence that scriptural sexual ethics are merely cultural and therefore negotiable now. The plain answer is that the marriage preceded the statute, that Scripture records it without embarrassment in the very books that contain the prohibition, and that the God who gives law also fixes when it binds. Abraham married his half-sister on the same footing. What the argument actually needs, and never supplies, is a reason to think the moral law of Lev 18 — against incest, adultery, homosexual practice, and child sacrifice — is up for revision because Israel's marriage customs were regulated in stages. The prohibitions of that chapter are grounded in creation and are addressed to the Gentile nations as well, which is why the land is said to spue them out for breaking them.

The other thing to name is what Amram is actually famous for, which is resisting a state order to kill a child. Pharaoh commanded that every son be cast into the river; Amram and Jochebed hid theirs and then floated him in a basket into the household of the man who had issued the decree. Hebrews commends it as faith and notes what it lacked: “they were not afraid of the king's commandment.” The Hebrew midwives had done the same and God built them houses. There is a limit to the obedience owed to the civil magistrate, and Scripture puts it exactly where the magistrate commands sin.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Amram (H6019), from 'am (H5971), people, and rum (H7311), to be high; Yokebed (H3115), Jochebed, “the LORD is glory”.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Amram (H6019) — Amram; eldest son of Kohath, head of the Amramites.
Hebrew Yokebed (H3115) — Jochebed; the first name in Scripture compounded with the covenant name.
Hebrew tsaphan (H6845) — to hide, treasure up; the verb of Exo 2:2, the three months of concealment.
Hebrew tebah (H8392) — an ark, chest; used only of Noah's vessel and of the bulrush basket.
Greek asteios (G791) — fair, comely; “a proper child” in Heb 11:23 and Act 7:20.
usage: “She bare him Aaron and Moses” — one household, the priesthood and the law.
“The children of Amram; Aaron, and Moses, and Miriam” — the Chronicler's roll.
“They were not afraid of the king's commandment” — the one deed Hebrews records of him.

pos: n. pl. (the given ones — temple servants of foreign descent assigned to assist the Levites, and among the first to come back from Babylon)
etymology: From Hebrew Nethinim, the passive participle of nathan, to give — literally “the given ones”, those donated to the service of the sanctuary. The KJV adds an English plural to a word already plural in Hebrew.
biblical_def: The Nethinims are the given ones: a body of temple servants, not of Israel by descent, appointed to the menial work of the house of God so that the Levites could attend to theirs. Their origin lies in two places. The Gibeonites were made “hewers of wood and drawers of water… for the house of my God” by Joshua; and Ezra records a later augmentation — “of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites” (Ezr 8:20). Their names in the registers are largely foreign. What matters is what happened to them. When Cyrus opened the way home, most of the exiles stayed in Babylon where they had houses and trades; and among the small company that went up were “all the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants… three hundred ninety and two” (Ezr 2:58). Slaves of the sanctuary walked back to a ruin to serve in it. They are listed with the priests and Levites as exempt from tribute by Artaxerxes' decree, they built their portion of the wall, they dwelt in Ophel by the water gate (Neh 3:26; Neh 11:21), and they sealed the covenant with Nehemiah. Descendants of the conquered, given to the house, and found at the door when the house was rebuilt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Nethinims as servants of the priests and Levites in the temple, given or devoted to that service, chiefly of the Gibeonites and other captives.
webster_full: NETHINIMS, n. plu. In Jewish antiquity, the servants of the priests and Levites in the temple.
The word signifies given or devoted, from a Hebrew verb to give.
They are supposed to have been the Gibeonites, made hewers of wood and drawers of water by Joshua.
David and the princes appointed others of them for the service of the Levites.
Many of them returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel and with Ezra, and dwelt in Ophel.
scriptures: Ezr 2:58
All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two.
Ezr 8:20
Also of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinims: all of them were expressed by name.
Neh 3:26
Moreover the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel, unto the place over against the water gate toward the east, and the tower that lieth out.
But the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel: and Ziha and Gispa were over the Nethinims.
corruption_summary: An order of temple servants drawn from a conquered people is read as religious slavery; Scripture treats their inclusion as mercy and records their names, their exemption, and their voluntary return.
corruption_paragraphs: The Nethinims are sometimes cited as evidence that Israel's religion sanctified a caste system. The details will not support it. Under the law a foreigner attached to the sanctuary was protected, provided for, and brought within the covenant community — the Gibeonites, having lied their way to a treaty, were placed at the altar of the God they had feared, and four centuries later Saul's attempt to destroy them brought a three-year famine on Israel. Artaxerxes exempted the Nethinims from toll, tribute, and custom along with the priests. Ezra records them as “expressed by name”, which is the opposite of how a slave register is kept. And the covenant of Neh 10 is sealed by “the Nethinims, and all they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God” — they are inside, by profession.

The principle to recover is what their name means. Nethinim is the passive of the verb “to give”: they are the given ones, men who did not give themselves but were given, and whose whole standing was that they belonged to the house. The New Testament says the same thing of the church in the words of Christ — “thine they were, and thou gavest them me” (Joh 17:6) — and of ministers, whom Paul calls “your servants for Jesus' sake” (2Co 4:5). Three hundred and ninety-two of them chose a ruined temple over a comfortable exile. That is what a given one looks like.
roots_summary: Hebrew Nethinim (H5411), the given ones, from nathan (H5414), to give; compare nethunim (Num 8:16), the Levites “wholly given” to the LORD.
roots_lines: Hebrew Nethinim (H5411) — Nethinims; temple servants, literally those who have been given.
Hebrew nathan (H5414) — to give, put, set; the root of the name and of Nathan, Jonathan, and Nethaniah.
Hebrew nethunim nethunim — “wholly given”; the doubled participle used of the Levites themselves (Num 8:16).
Hebrew 'Ophel (H6077) — Ophel, the swelling or hill south of the temple mount where they lived.
Hebrew chotebe 'etsim we-sho'abe mayim — hewers of wood and drawers of water; the Gibeonite office (Jos 9:23).
usage: “All the Nethinims… three hundred ninety and two” — the servants who came home.
“Whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites” — an order with a charter.
“The Nethinims dwelt in Ophel” — quarters beside the house they served.

pos: n. (prince of Judah in the wilderness, father-in-law of Aaron and forefather of David and of Christ — a link in the royal genealogy)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Amminadab, “my kinsman is noble” or “the people are willing”, from 'am, people or kinsman, and nadab, to be willing, to offer freely. Matthew spells it Aminadab in the Greek.
biblical_def: Amminadab stands at a junction where the priesthood and the throne cross. He was of the tribe of Judah, and his daughter Elisheba married the high priest: “Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Naashon, to wife” (Exo 6:23) — so the entire Aaronic priesthood descends from a Judahite mother. His son Nahshon was the prince of Judah in the wilderness, named first of the twelve at the numbering — “Of Judah; Nahshon the son of Amminadab” (Num 1:7) — the man whose standard led the march and who brought the first offering at the dedication of the altar. And the line runs on to the throne: “Ram begat Amminadab, and Amminadab begat Nahshon, and Nahshon begat Salmon” (Rut 4:19-20), Salmon begat Boaz of Rahab, Boaz begat Obed of Ruth, and Obed was the grandfather of David. Matthew places him in the genealogy of the Lord Jesus without comment: “Aram begat Aminadab; and Aminadab begat Naasson” (Mat 1:4). Nothing Amminadab said is recorded and nothing he did. He is a name that carried the promise through the wilderness generation, from the brickyards of Egypt to the door of Canaan.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Amminadab; in sacred history he is a prince of the tribe of Judah, father of Nahshon and of Elisheba the wife of Aaron.
webster_full: AMMINADAB, n. A prince of the tribe of Judah in the time of Moses; the name signifies my kinsman is noble.
His daughter Elisheba was married to Aaron the high priest.
His son Nahshon was captain of the children of Judah in the wilderness.
He is named in the genealogy of David in the book of Ruth.
He is named also in the genealogy of our Lord in the first chapter of Matthew and the third of Luke.
scriptures: Exo 6:23
And Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Naashon, to wife; and she bare him Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
Num 1:7
Of Judah; Nahshon the son of Amminadab.
Rut 4:19
And Hezron begat Ram, and Ram begat Amminadab,
Mat 1:4
And Aram begat Aminadab; and Aminadab begat Naasson; and Naasson begat Salmon;
corruption_summary: Genealogies are skipped as dead lists; Matthew opens the New Testament with one because the gospel depends on a promise made to particular men and kept through particular sons.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is why the Bible keeps lists of fathers. The promise of Gen 3:15 is about a seed; the promise to Abraham is about a seed; the promise to David is about a son. Every name in the chain is the promise not failing in that generation. Matthew therefore begins his gospel not with a doctrine but with a register, and the first Christian readers, who knew what a Jewish genealogy was for, understood the claim being made before a single event was narrated. To skip the list is to skip the argument.

The second thing Amminadab supplies is the crossing of the two lines. His daughter married into the priesthood and his son led the tribe of the kings; his descendants include both Aaron's sons and David's father. Israel kept priest and king strictly apart — Uzziah was struck with leprosy for taking a censer — and yet the offices were meant to meet, and Scripture says where: in a priest after the order of Melchizedek, who is both. “For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood” (Heb 7:14). Amminadab's family is a small early hint that the two crowns belong on one head.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Amminadab (H5992), from 'am (H5971), kinsman, and nadab (H5068), to volunteer, offer willingly; Greek Aminadab (G284).
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Amminadab (H5992) — Amminadab, “my kinsman is noble”.
Hebrew nadab (H5068) — to impel, to volunteer; the root of nedabah, a freewill offering.
Hebrew Nachshon (H5177) — Nahshon, his son, prince of Judah and first to offer at the altar (Num 7:12).
Hebrew 'Elisheba' (H472) — Elisheba, his daughter, wife of Aaron; the Hebrew form of Elisabeth.
Greek Aminadab (G284) — Aminadab; the spelling in the genealogies of Matthew and Luke.
usage: “Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab” — the priesthood married into Judah.
“Nahshon the son of Amminadab” — the standard that led the march.
“Aminadab begat Naasson” — a wilderness name in the line of Christ.

pos: n. (a priestly name of the house of Eli and afterwards of the house of Zadok — standing at the hinge where one priestly line was cut off and another established)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Achituwb, “my brother is goodness” or “brother of goodness”, from 'ach, brother, and tob, good. At least two and probably three priests bear it.
biblical_def: Ahitub is a name that sits exactly on the fault line of the Old Testament priesthood. The first Ahitub is of the doomed house: “Ahiah, the son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli” (1Sa 14:3) — grandson of Eli, nephew of the child born the day the ark was taken. His son Ahimelech gave David the shewbread and Goliath's sword at Nob, and for it Doeg the Edomite informed on him — “I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub” (1Sa 22:9) — and Saul had eighty-five priests killed in a day, which fulfilled the word spoken against Eli's house. Only Abiathar escaped. The second Ahitub is of the house that replaced it: “Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests” (2Sa 8:17), and the Chronicler traces the descent plainly — “Ahitub begat Zadok, and Zadok begat Ahimaaz” (1Ch 6:8). Zadok stayed with David when Absalom rose and with Solomon when Adonijah rose; Abiathar did not, and was thrust out from being priest, “that he might fulfil the word of the LORD which he spake concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh”. One name, two houses, and a warning between them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Ahitub; in sacred history the name belongs to a grandson of Eli and to the father of Zadok the priest.
webster_full: AHITUB, n. The son of Phinehas and grandson of Eli, high priest of the line of Ithamar.
The name signifies brother of goodness.
His son Ahimelech was slain by Doeg at the command of Saul, with fourscore and five priests of Nob.
Another Ahitub, of the line of Eleazar, was the father of Zadok, who was made priest in the room of Abiathar.
In him the high priesthood returned from the house of Ithamar to the house of Eleazar.
scriptures: Then answered Doeg the Edomite, which was set over the servants of Saul, and said, I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub.
And Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests; and Seraiah was the scribe;
And Ahitub begat Zadok, and Zadok begat Ahimaaz,
Behold, the days come, that I will cut off thine arm, and the arm of thy father's house, that there shall not be an old man in thine house.
corruption_summary: Sacred office is treated as a possession secured by ordination and lineage; the house of Eli held both and was cut off, because God's word to it turned on how its sons behaved.
corruption_paragraphs: The house of Eli had everything an office can give. It held the high priesthood, the ark was in its keeping at Shiloh, and the succession was hereditary and unquestioned. What it did not have was sons who feared God: Hophni and Phinehas took the flesh by force and lay with the women at the door of the tabernacle, and their father restrained them with words and no more. The sentence is one of the most searching in Scripture — “them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed” (1Sa 2:30). It was executed in stages: the ark taken, Eli dead at the gate, the slaughter of the priests at Nob under Saul, and finally Abiathar deposed by Solomon. Ordination secures nothing. A minister's standing is not his credentials, and a church's continuance is not its charter.

The second matter is Doeg, because he is the mechanism. He was “detained before the LORD” at Nob on the day David came — present at the sanctuary, observing worship, and taking notes for the king. The informer is a permanent figure in the church's history, and Psa 52, written about this incident, describes him exactly: a tongue devising mischiefs like a sharp razor, a man who “trusted in the abundance of his riches” rather than in God. That psalm ends where the priesthood ended up: “I am like a green olive tree in the house of God: I trust in the mercy of God for ever and ever.”
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Achituwb (H285), from 'ach (H251), brother, and tob (H2896), good; Tsadoq (H6659), Zadok, righteous.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Achituwb (H285) — Ahitub, “my brother is goodness”; borne in both priestly houses.
Hebrew tob (H2896) — good; the word of Gen 1, and the second element of the name.
Hebrew Tsadoq (H6659) — Zadok, “righteous”; his son, from whom the Zadokite priesthood descends.
Hebrew 'Ebyathar (H54) — Abiathar, “the father of abundance”; the last priest of Eli's line.
Hebrew Nob (H5011) — Nob, the priests' city where the tabernacle stood and where they were slain.
usage: “Ahimelech the son of Ahitub” — the priest Doeg informed against.
“Zadok the son of Ahitub” — the house that took the office.
“Ahitub begat Zadok” — the line that held the sanctuary to the exile.

pos: n. (the Levite of mount Ephraim, husband of Hannah and father of Samuel — a man of yearly worship in a corrupt sanctuary)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Elqanah, “God has created” or “God has possessed”, from 'El, God, and qanah, to acquire, create, or purchase — the same verb Eve uses at the birth of Cain and Melchizedek uses of God as “possessor of heaven and earth”.
biblical_def: Elkanah opens the books of Samuel: “Now there was a certain man of Ramathaimzophim, of mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah” (1Sa 1:1). Chronicles shows him to be a Levite of the family of Kohath dwelling in Ephraimite territory. He had two wives, Peninnah with children and Hannah without, and the household was miserable with it — which is the plainest possible commentary on a practice the patriarchs and judges fell into and which Scripture never once shows going well. What Elkanah did do, year by year, was go up to worship: to Shiloh, where Hophni and Phinehas were defiling the offerings and the women at the door, and where the word of the LORD was precious and there was no open vision. He kept coming. He gave Hannah a worthy portion, and to her grief he answered with the tenderest and most inadequate sentence a husband ever spoke: “Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?” (1Sa 1:8). When she vowed and prayed and the LORD remembered her (1Sa 1:19), Elkanah ratified the vow and let her keep the child until he was weaned, and then gave up his firstborn son to the very sanctuary that was rotting. Eli blessed them, “the LORD give thee seed of this woman for the loan which is lent to the LORD” (1Sa 2:20), and God gave them five more.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Elkanah; in sacred history he is a Levite of mount Ephraim, the husband of Hannah and Peninnah and the father of Samuel the prophet.
webster_full: ELKANAH, n. A Hebrew name signifying God hath possessed or created.
The father of Samuel, a Levite of the family of Kohath, dwelling at Ramathaim-zophim in mount Ephraim.
He went up yearly to worship and to sacrifice unto the Lord of hosts in Shiloh.
He had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah, and loved Hannah though she was barren.
He suffered her vow to stand, and brought the child Samuel to the house of the Lord when he was weaned.
scriptures: Now there was a certain man of Ramathaimzophim, of mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephrathite:
Then said Elkanah her husband to her, Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?
And they rose up in the morning early, and worshipped before the LORD, and returned, and came to their house to Ramah: and Elkanah knew Hannah his wife; and the LORD remembered her.
And Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, and said, The LORD give thee seed of this woman for the loan which is lent to the LORD. And they went unto their own home.
corruption_summary: Elkanah's two wives are cited as biblical warrant for polygamy; Scripture records it and then shows the house it made — a rival provoking a barren woman to tears year after year.
corruption_paragraphs: That the Bible narrates polygamy is not the same as approving it, and 1 Samuel 1 is a good place to see the difference. The creation ordinance is fixed at Gen 2:24, one man and one woman, and the Lord Jesus goes back to it and says “from the beginning it was not so” (Mat 19:8). Every polygamous household in Scripture is a case study in misery: Sarah and Hagar, Leah and Rachel, David's sons, Solomon's heart turned away, and here Peninnah “provoked her sore, for to make her fret” and Hannah weeping and not eating. The dictionary holds monogamous marriage as the only lawful union, and the office of elder requires “the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2). Where Scripture describes, it is not therefore prescribing.

The second thing Elkanah teaches is a hard one about corrupt churches. Shiloh in his day was a scandal: the priests were thieves and adulterers, and 1Sa 3:1 says the word of the LORD was precious and there was no open vision. Elkanah went up anyway, year by year, and offered, and worshipped, and his wife prayed there, and God answered from that defiled sanctuary and raised up the prophet who would replace its priesthood. The lesson is not that corruption is tolerable — God destroyed Eli's house for it. The lesson is that God's ordinances remain His even when the men administering them are wicked, and that the reformer He raised up was born to a woman who kept turning up to pray.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Elqanah (H511), from 'El (H410), God, and qanah (H7069), to acquire, create, possess; Shiloh (H7887).
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Elqanah (H511) — Elkanah, “God has possessed”; borne by several Kohathite Levites.
Hebrew qanah (H7069) — to get, acquire, create; the verb behind “possessor of heaven and earth” (Gen 14:19).
Hebrew Ramathayim Tsophim (H7436) — Ramathaim-zophim, the double height of the watchers, his town.
Hebrew sha'al (H7592) — to ask; the verb behind Samuel's name and Hannah's petition (1Sa 1:20).
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember; “the LORD remembered her” (1Sa 1:19), covenant action, not recollection.
usage: “A certain man of Ramathaimzophim… and his name was Elkanah” — how the books of Samuel begin.
“Am not I better to thee than ten sons?” — a tender question that missed the point.
“The loan which is lent to the LORD” — Eli's blessing on the giving up of a son.

pos: n. (the father of Caleb the Kenezite — a patronymic repeated fifteen times, always attached to the man who wholly followed the LORD)
etymology: From Hebrew Yephunneh, probably “he will be prepared” or “he will be turned”, from panah, to turn or face. He is called a Kenezite, which points to a house grafted into Judah rather than sprung from it.
biblical_def: Jephunneh is known entirely through his son. Fifteen times Scripture writes “Caleb the son of Jephunneh”, beginning with the roll of the twelve spies: “Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh” (Num 13:6). When ten came back with the evil report and the congregation talked of stoning, “Joshua the son of Nun, and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, which were of them that searched the land, rent their clothes” (Num 14:6). Forty-five years later the old man came to Gilgal and claimed his mountain: “Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite said unto him, Thou knowest the thing that the LORD said unto Moses the man of God concerning me and thee in Kadeshbarnea” (Jos 14:6), and the account closes with the reason for it all — “Hebron therefore became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite unto this day, because that he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel” (Jos 14:14). The designation Kenezite matters. Kenaz is listed among the dukes of Edom, and the likeliest reading is that Jephunneh's house was of foreign stock incorporated into Judah. If so, the two men of that whole generation who believed God enough to enter the land were a Levite's pupil from Ephraim and the son of a naturalised Edomite.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Jephunneh; in sacred history he is the father of Caleb the Kenezite, one of the two spies who brought a good report of the land.
webster_full: JEPHUNNEH, n. The father of Caleb, of the tribe of Judah, called the Kenezite.
The name is thought to signify he that beholds, or he shall be prepared.
His son was one of the twelve sent to search the land of Canaan.
Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun alone of that generation entered the land.
Hebron was given him for an inheritance because he wholly followed the Lord God of Israel.
scriptures: Num 13:6
Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh.
Num 14:6
And Joshua the son of Nun, and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, which were of them that searched the land, rent their clothes:
Jos 14:6

Then the children of Judah came unto Joshua in Gilgal: and Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite said unto him, Thou knowest the thing that the LORD said unto Moses the man of God concerning me and thee in Kadeshbarnea.
Hebron therefore became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite unto this day, because that he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel.
corruption_summary: The Kenezite designation is used to argue that Israel's ancestry claims are fiction; the text volunteers the foreign stock, which is not how a fabricated purity myth behaves.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The point worth holding is what Scripture is willing to say about itself. If the Old Testament were the ethnic charter myth it is often called, it would not repeatedly attach the word Kenezite to the greatest hero of the conquest generation, nor put Rahab of Jericho and Ruth of Moab into the ancestry of David, nor number a mixed multitude among those who came out of Egypt. The covenant line runs by promise and faith, not by blood purity, and the text says so in the middle of the conquest narrative that is supposed to be its most tribal section.

The principle in the phrase itself is the one to preach. “He wholly followed the LORD God of Israel” is said of Caleb six times, and the Hebrew is mille' 'acharey, literally “he filled up after” the LORD — he followed all the way, left nothing behind, held nothing back. It is the answer to the ten spies, who saw the same giants and the same walled cities and reported truly about both, and then drew the conclusion of unbelief. Faith is not the denial of the giants. Caleb asked for the hill country with the Anakim on it, at eighty-five, and said “if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out” (Jos 14:12).
roots_summary: Hebrew Yephunneh (H3312), from panah (H6437), to turn, to face; Qenizzi (H7074), Kenezite; Kaleb (H3612), Caleb.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yephunneh (H3312) — Jephunneh; father of Caleb, and of a second man in the line of Asher.
Hebrew panah (H6437) — to turn, to look toward; the likely root of the name.
Hebrew Qenizzi (H7074) — Kenezite; from Kenaz, a name found among the dukes of Edom (Gen 36:15).
Hebrew Kaleb (H3612) — Caleb; the same consonants as the word for dog, and so a name of humility.
Hebrew male' 'acharey — to fill up after, to follow fully; the phrase rendered “wholly followed”.
usage: “Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh” — one of twelve sent out.
“Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenezite” — a foreign house inside the tribe of the kings.
“Because that he wholly followed the LORD” — the reason Hebron changed hands.

pos: n. (the Ephraimite father of Joshua — a patronymic so constant that the successor of Moses is scarcely ever named without it)
etymology: From Hebrew Nun, probably from a root meaning to propagate, to continue, or to flourish — the same word is the name of the fourteenth Hebrew letter. He is of the tribe of Ephraim, grandson of Elishama the prince (1Ch 7:26-27).
biblical_def: Nun is the father of Joshua, and Scripture will hardly let the son be mentioned without him: “Joshua the son of Nun” occurs some thirty times, from the wilderness to the book of Judges. He first appears when the young man will not leave the tent: “his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle” (Exo 33:11). He is one of the twelve spies, and it is at the sending that Moses changes his name: “Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua” (Num 13:16) — from “salvation” to “the LORD is salvation”, the Hebrew name of which Jesus is the Greek. He and Caleb alone of that generation crossed Jordan. Moses laid hands on him: “Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him: and the children of Israel hearkened unto him” (Deu 34:9), and the next book opens on the succession — “the LORD spake unto Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' minister” (Jos 1:1). Of Nun himself nothing is recorded. He is an Ephraimite who died in Egypt or in the wilderness, and whose name is written into the title of the man who took Israel into the land.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Nun as a person; in sacred history he is the father of Joshua, of the tribe of Ephraim, and the name is also that of a letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
webster_full: NUN, n. The father of Joshua, of the tribe of Ephraim, descended from Elishama the prince of that tribe.
The name is thought to signify continuance or perpetuity.
Nun is also the name of the fourteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
The son of Nun was called Oshea, and Moses named him Jehoshua.
He was Moses' minister, and succeeded him in the leading of Israel into Canaan.
scriptures: And the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend. And he turned again into the camp: but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle.
These are the names of the men which Moses sent to spy out the land. And Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua.
Deu 34:9
And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him: and the children of Israel hearkened unto him, and did as the LORD commanded Moses.
Jos 1:1
Now after the death of Moses the servant of the LORD it came to pass, that the LORD spake unto Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' minister, saying,
corruption_summary: Succession in the church is treated as an institutional mechanism; Joshua was prepared for it by years of attending on Moses in the tabernacle before any hands were laid on him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how the Bible produces a successor. Long before Deu 34:9 and the laying on of hands, there is Exo 33:11: a young man who “departed not out of the tabernacle” when the great man had gone back to the camp. Joshua was formed by proximity to the presence of God and by years of ordinary attendance on Moses — carrying, waiting, going up the mountain part of the way, standing at the door. Then came the commission, and the office was laid on a man already shaped for it. The New Testament pattern is identical: Timothy attended Paul, was proved, and only then received the laying on of the hands of the presbytery, and the rule stands — “Lay hands suddenly on no man” (1Ti 5:22).

The renaming in Num 13:16 is worth a second look. Oshea means salvation; Moses prefixes the covenant name and makes it “the LORD is salvation”. The point is not decorative. Twelve men were about to go into the land and ten of them would come back reckoning by their own strength, and the leader of the two who did not was sent out with a name that answered the question of the whole expedition. The Greek of that name is Iesous, Jesus, and Hebrews notes the type: the Joshua who gave them rest in Canaan did not give the true rest, so “there remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9).
roots_summary: Hebrew Nun (H5126), Nun; Hoshea' (H1954), Oshea, salvation; Yehoshua' (H3091), Joshua, the LORD is salvation; Greek Iesous (G2424).
roots_lines: Hebrew Nun (H5126) — Nun; an Ephraimite, father of Joshua, of the house of Elishama.
Hebrew Hoshea' (H1954) — Oshea, Hosea; salvation, deliverance — Joshua's original name.
Hebrew Yehoshua' (H3091) — Jehoshua, Joshua; “the LORD is salvation”, the name Moses gave him.
Greek Iesous (G2424) — Jesus; the Greek of the same name, used of Joshua in Act 7:45 and Heb 4:8.
Hebrew mesharet (H8334) — a minister, attendant; Joshua's standing title before he was leader.
usage: “His servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man” — the apprenticeship at the tent door.
“Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua” — a name changed before a hard errand.
“Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' minister” — how the book of the conquest opens.

pos: n. (the man who with Aaron held up Moses' hands at Rephidim, and was left with him to judge Israel — grandfather of Bezaleel the craftsman)
etymology: From Hebrew Chuwr, of uncertain meaning; a hole or a cave, or possibly white linen, or a connexion with the Egyptian Horus has been proposed. He is of the tribe of Judah, and Jewish tradition makes him Miriam's husband, which Scripture does not say.
biblical_def: Hur appears at three moments and then vanishes, and every appearance is one of support. At Rephidim, while Joshua fought Amalek in the valley, “Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill” (Exo 17:10), and when the rod grew heavy in the old man's arms, “they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun” (Exo 17:12). Israel prevailed. Second, when Moses went up Sinai and would be gone forty days, he left the government of the camp in two pairs of hands: “behold, Aaron and Hur are with you: if any man have any matters to do, let him come unto them” (Exo 24:14) — and it was during that absence that Aaron made the calf, with no word of what Hur did or failed to do. Third, his grandson is the man God fills with the Spirit for the work of the sanctuary: “I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah” (Exo 31:2). Chronicles makes his line the founders of Bethlehem. A man who held up somebody else's arms, and whose grandson built the tabernacle.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Hur as a person; in sacred history he is a chief man of Judah who with Aaron stayed up the hands of Moses in the battle with Amalek.
webster_full: HUR, n. A man of the tribe of Judah, associated with Aaron in the government of the people.
With Aaron he held up the hands of Moses upon the hill while Joshua fought with Amalek.
He was left with Aaron to judge the people while Moses was in the mount.
He was the grandfather of Bezaleel, the chief workman of the tabernacle.
Another Hur was one of the five kings of Midian slain with Balaam.
scriptures: So Joshua did as Moses had said to him, and fought with Amalek: and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.

But Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.
And he said unto the elders, Tarry ye here for us, until we come again unto you: and, behold, Aaron and Hur are with you: if any man have any matters to do, let him come unto them.
Exo 31:2
See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah:
corruption_summary: Rephidim is preached as a lesson in teamwork; the text is about intercession — the battle turned on a held-up rod, not on the men in the valley.
corruption_paragraphs: The Amalek narrative is a favourite of motivational preaching, reduced to the moral that leaders need support and nobody wins alone. That is true and it is not what the chapter is about. The passage makes an outrageous claim: while the rod was up Israel prevailed, and when it went down Amalek prevailed, and the fighting in the valley made no difference either way. The strength of the arm was irrelevant; the sign of the rod — the same rod that struck the Nile and divided the sea — was everything. Moses built an altar and called it Jehovah-nissi, the LORD my banner. What Aaron and Hur did was not encouragement but participation in intercession, and that is the standing office of the church: “the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (Jas 5:16).

The second thing about Hur is a silence, and it should be handled honestly. Moses left Aaron and Hur jointly in charge, and while he was gone the calf was made. Aaron's part is recorded in detail and his excuse is preserved for our shame. Of Hur nothing is said. He may have resisted and been overruled; he may have gone along; later Jewish legend has him killed for opposing it, which Scripture does not support. What is certain is that being placed in authority alongside a stronger man is no protection, and that when a congregation turns, second-chair officers are tested exactly as the first is. The one thing Hur is remembered for is holding an arm up. It is a better epitaph than most.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chuwr (H2354), Hur; Betsal'el (H1212), Bezaleel, “in the shadow of God”; Yehovah-nissi (H3071), the LORD my banner.
roots_lines: Hebrew Chuwr (H2354) — Hur; a chief man of Judah, grandfather of Bezaleel.
Hebrew Betsal'el (H1212) — Bezaleel, “in the shadow of God”; the first man Scripture says was filled with the Spirit of God, for craftsmanship (Exo 31:3).
Hebrew Yehovah-nissi (H3071) — Jehovah-nissi, “the LORD my banner”; the altar Moses built after the battle.
Hebrew tamak (H8551) — to hold up, uphold, sustain; the verb of Exo 17:12.
Hebrew 'emunah (H530) — steadiness, faithfulness; “his hands were steady”, the noun elsewhere rendered faith.
usage: “Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill” — three men above a battle.
“Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands” — the ministry of holding an arm.
“Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur” — a grandson called by name to build.
